Is it a give and take when a client comes to you wanting to accomplish X and you suggest Y?

Jordan Isenstadt: Clients come to us asking for a mixed bag of things and aren't sure what the tactics should be. Our expertise is in earned media — there's earned, owned, paid, and social, the PESO model. Earned media is our specialty. That's trying to get media outlets — podcasts, print, broadcast, radio — to cover our clients without paying them, as compared to an ad, where the client pays the outlet. With earned media there's validation and credibility that comes with it compared to an ad. The truth is, if you're looking for new customers, B2B or B2C, you probably need all of it — earned, paid, and owned (your website, blog, social media). The question is the right balance. In cannabis, because of federal prohibition, there's less you can do from a traditional marketing standpoint — regulations differ state to state, publishers differ market to market, Google is its own beast. That's what makes PR and earned media so important in cannabis — one of the most viable options to get attention to your brand. But clients often just say 'we need marketing' without understanding the distinctions. We can help with all of it, but our historic heart is PR and earned media.

Kellan Finney: The reason I asked is because aligning expectations with success is so critical — if a client expects sales and you deliver earned media placements, there can be a disconnect.

Jordan Isenstadt: Right, PR and earned media don't always immediately lead to sales — it's cumulative. If you're doing PR, you also need to be doing marketing, have a great website, a great social feed, and engage with influencers. One frustrating thing in PR is it's hard to draw a direct correlation between an article hit and sales — it's one piece of the pie. But we'd argue that in cannabis it's an outsized slice of that pie.

Kellan Finney: The way I think about it is when you see 'as seen in' on a website — New York Times, Vice, Forbes, Wall Street Journal — that's earned media, and it's a validation touchpoint that builds comfort with a brand. But another area where PR is extremely beneficial is messaging, because cannabis carries stigmas — it's not a normal product like McDonald's you can just advertise without issue. Messaging is critical given the diversity of customers.

Jordan Isenstadt: One hundred percent. PR is also about storytelling. A big part of what we do with any client, usually in the first few weeks of an engagement, is build a strategy based on a narrative and a story. Everyone in cannabis has a unique and interesting story, and people are looking for authentic connection to authentic brands. It's critical we work with clients to figure out their story and how to best disseminate it — key messages we repeat across different outlets, sometimes with a slightly different angle. Compared to other PR practices, cannabis PR is part of an overall mission of normalizing and destigmatizing cannabis — through stories like a cannabis lawyer who's a mom doing amazing things, a couple who met through the legacy market and now own a dispensary, or a certified ganjier working with a former grocery chain CEO to build a unique cannabis store. Every client has special sauce, and the mission is to get people to recognize the legitimacy and utility of cannabis and continue destigmatizing it.

Bryan Fields: When you bring new clients in and start understanding their story, is it like — hey, let's grab drinks, get them warmed up? What's the playbook for authentic interaction with a new client?

Jordan Isenstadt: Every client is different — you've got to read the vibe, read the room. It's like dating. Early on I signed a New York City client planning to apply for an adult-use dispensary. I went to his CBD store, we went to the back room, I had the contract before he signed it, he rolled a joint, we broke bread, got to know each other, then he signed, and we went into the storytelling meeting where he told me his background — like discovering as a teenager he was allergic to alcohol, getting very sick when friends offered him alcohol, then discovering cannabis and all the amazing things it did for him. That's an example of a meeting where we got to the story over a joint or a bong rip. Some clients it's a Zoom call if they're not local; some come into the office. We've been working with a lot of dispensary owners lately, so we'll go to the dispensary even if it's a construction zone, because we want to feel them out, get the vibe, learn who they are. You have to get into their brain — especially because we're often writing statements or op-eds on their behalf, so we need to learn how they think and put words together that sound authentically like them. The first few weeks are critical. PR is a partnership — sometimes clients tell us a bunch of stuff and say 'now just make stuff happen,' but that's not how it works. The best partnerships have a constant flow of information — regular calls, texts, ideas going back and forth. You need a willing partner who's ready to give you the information to build the campaign, otherwise it feels hollow.

Kellan Finney: It's got to be such a challenging balance — some individuals have been hesitant to share details in the past, then you need to bring them to the forefront and craft a story that's clear and emotion-evoking. In New York, since the market is brand new, people are making first-time decisions on which dispensary or brand to choose, and sometimes it comes down to the story — packaging, color, font, or the wording on the back that connects, like a family farm that's been growing for generations. Those small details require back-and-forth partnership that people don't always recognize as intricate to success.

Jordan Isenstadt: Clients come in all shapes and sizes. Corporate cannabis is a very different animal than some of the players we deal with in New York now. Having worked with Curaleaf, Ayr Wellness, and other larger players, it's really corporate PR — you just happen to be selling weed — and most of those folks have had C-suite experience elsewhere, so they get the marketing apparatus. The challenge comes with smaller, newer players. In New York specifically, because of how the program was structured, the first store owners were largely justice-involved, social equity licensees from the legacy market — some in it thirty years, some until just last year. Those more recently in the legacy market are used to operating in the shadows, not talking about themselves, so getting them to talk openly about selling weed, building a team, their tech, their lease — it's a hump to get over and takes time. Some jump on it quickly, some need training — that's a big part of what we do, meeting the client where they're at. Some need minimal media training; some are raw and need real shaping, even though they all have an authentic story — it's about giving them the right words. Some clients need step-by-step written messaging, and some will put messaging together but probably never read it.

Bryan Fields: Another topic that's a first for so many people is cannabis and parenting. I think that topic is about to get blown open — there are a lot of firsts happening. As the stigma continues moving in the right direction, parents and society need to figure out whether this is on par with alcohol, whether it's fair and safe, and where the conversation goes.

Jordan Isenstadt: Great question, and I have a complicated context for the answer. Personally, I first tried cannabis in the mid-'90s, at 15, at summer camp — not saying anyone should do that, that's just my origin story. I came home and told my dad I'd tried it and liked it, and he said, 'We'll get some and sample it together.' So I had a very open parent. A couple years later my mother, who was divorced from my dad, also caught wind of it, and by college I was sampling with her too. Now as a father, I have a 12-year-old and an 8-year-old — really interesting ages, because my 8-year-old doesn't really understand what I do, but my 12-year-old does; she knows kids come into middle school with vapes, hears things, and hears me talk about cannabis since I work from home half the week. She's asked me questions, and I've settled on telling her cannabis is a plant, it's for wellness, and we can talk more when she's older — though I'll probably have to massage that line soon. What's different about my childhood versus my kids' is they're growing up in a world where cannabis is state-legal in a way prior generations never experienced. We're in a weird golden age where my kids ask 'what's that smell' in New York City, or 'why is Rick and Morty in there' referring to illicit stores. I'm trying to show them the more responsible side. Part of normalizing and destigmatizing is moving away from stoner iconography; illicit stores will eventually shut down, and we need to think of cannabis less like alcohol in terms of bodily impact, but similarly as a regulated, age-gated product. Data shows legal cannabis usually decreases minor usage because it becomes less interesting once it's legal. I've thought about writing a children's book on how to talk to your kids about cannabis — a half-baked idea, but someone needs to do it. We need proactive, responsible conversations, not scare tactics, especially since things like kids getting into parents' gummy stashes are a real, sporadic issue. I've wondered if gummies as a formulation even make sense for a household with kids — maybe it should just be pill form, since gummies feel too kid-friendly.

Kellan Finney: Gummies clearly sell well for cash flow, but they're also easy for kids to eat since kids love candy. Given that, should parents proactively approach the topic at a certain age, like with cell phones, or wait for the kid to bring it up?

Jordan Isenstadt: I'm in a unique position where it's an unavoidable conversation in my household. I do think middle school — sixth, seventh, eighth grade — is when kids start learning from peers and from their phones. So proactive conversation is probably the way to go, though you also have to know your kid and how they'll react. It might make sense to bundle it into a broader conversation about alcohol and being responsible with substances, what they are, their impact on the body, and what peers might be saying. Knowledge is power. This is a unique moment — some kids' parents will completely ignore it, some will proactively address it, maybe even consume with their kids like my parents did with me. I look fondly on those early experiences with my parents; it showed me it could be handled safely and responsibly — don't drive after, etc. There's a real opportunity for this generation of parents to change the narrative, though I don't know what parents in the '30s said to their kids after alcohol prohibition ended — maybe there are interesting parallels worth exploring.

Bryan Fields: I think you made a ton of really good points, and there's a fine balance. It reminds me of the DARE program in school — them telling me how bad it was actually encouraged me more than deterred me. If they'd spoken more about responsibility, like you said, it would help define what's normalized and expected. A lot of people experienced alcohol, crossed the line into too much, and learned boundaries the hard way. There's also the 'it's five o'clock somewhere' mentality — we've normalized alcohol to the point people casually grab a drink after work. I wonder if cannabis — a joint, a THC beverage, an edible — could follow a similar pattern for stress relief, except it's more discreet since there's no visible drink involved, which might prolong that period of normalization. Either way, there's no single right answer, but being honest and helping define boundaries might improve on what the previous generation did with us.

Jordan Isenstadt: That's a great point — DARE, Mothers Against Drunk Driving, those programs — our generation dealt with learning that as kids, and now we're here with our own kids growing up in a world where cannabis is legal. It's our opportunity to change the narrative — parent comes home, instead of pouring a whiskey, grabs a cannabis beverage or edible.

Kellan Finney: Do you think schools should play a role in that conversation?

Jordan Isenstadt: I'd love to think schools should play a role, but I don't really know what that would look like — I'm not sure what a school's programming on alcohol even consists of beyond 'don't drink and drive.' I don't know if schools can have a formal role there; I think it's really on the parents.

Bryan Fields: It's a fascinating conversation. I think continued education and helping people learn the differences and boundaries will allow for healthy conversations and honesty, so kids growing up understand responsible decision-making is critical as an adult, whether it's alcohol, cannabis, or another substance.

Jordan Isenstadt: One hundred percent, it's all about responsible use — having a lock box, keeping it stowed away, not driving after consuming, being a model for your kids that you can consume responsibly, much like with alcohol. Right now there's still a lot of talk about cannabis and fentanyl and other scary myths, and that was the problem with DARE and MADD — scare tactics don't work. We need to move away from scare tactics and be real — this is part of the world, people consume these products. Cannabis sales recently eclipsed alcohol sales in the news — that's the paradigm we're living in now. It's about promoting responsible use.

Bryan Fields: I agree, and it's case by case. Growing up, I knew kids whose parents wanted their first beer to be with them, teaching responsible drinking, and other parents took the opposite approach — you can't say one option works better across the board, it depends on knowing your kid.

Jordan Isenstadt: I have some European family, and that's what I was thinking too — they start drinking at like 14 there. That's how you destigmatize it, it becomes normalized, like having wine at dinner and then you're done. Whereas my own cannabis origin story felt so wrong — smoking out of an apple in the woods, then coming home and not being able to say anything, when really I'd have loved to just tell my dad. If it were normalized like a beverage at dinner, it wouldn't have to be a big deal — that's the future we need to get to.

Bryan Fields: I got caught smoking cannabis in high school, Jordan, and my parents decided I needed to take weekly drug tests for the rest of high school.

Jordan Isenstadt: That's one way of doing things.

Bryan Fields: We can have a conversation like that offline. Slightly switching gears, Jordan — dream smoking session, three people, dead or alive?

Jordan Isenstadt: I've been thinking about this one for a while. I'm a big Mets fan, 1986 was my team, so I'd put Dwight 'Doc' Gooden in my rotation. I'd put George Washington, because he grew hemp and I think he was smoking weed. And my late father, who I was talking about earlier — I'd do anything to smoke another joint with him. So Doc, George, and Gary — those are my picks.

Bryan Fields: What is the most expensive lesson you've ever learned?

Jordan Isenstadt: I spent many years working in government with a vision that I'd work in government my whole career and change things from the inside — I had political ambitions, wanted to work in the White House, maybe run for office. Seeing the slowness of government, at a certain point I had to hang it up. The expensive part is I spent about a decade on low government salaries before finally getting to the private side. I concluded I was better off working from the outside to influence things, and the cannabis work has really shown that a lot can be done from the outside.

Bryan Fields: True or false — you take part in a secret meeting of the minds on the Monday of MJBizCon every year?

Jordan Isenstadt: True statement, for the last two or three years running, soon to be three. This handsome crew gets together over espresso martinis at some point in the evening in Las Vegas on the Monday, and it's a great way to get things started. Our secret's out now.

Bryan Fields: Prediction time — what event or moment would signify that cannabis stigma is no longer here?

Jordan Isenstadt: It has to be federal legalization. Rescheduling is important, a step in the right direction, an acknowledgment of medical utility, but it won't change most hearts and minds — most people won't even know about it. Safe banking will be a big moment, when banks can accept cannabis cash. But until federal prohibition policy changes, I don't think we'll ever be at full normalization.

Kellan Finney: I agree with everything Jordan said, but for me the biggest moment will be when a Wells Fargo or Bank of America actually invests significant capital into one of the larger entities — because all these other milestones are steps toward the industry operating as a normal American capitalist business with access to financial institutions.

Bryan Fields: I'm in alignment with both, but I think the more culturally defining moment will be the Super Bowl — the moment you see a weed commercial during the Super Bowl. There'll be shock initially, but momentum will build after that, because people will realize it's normal, the old stigma and messaging were wrong, and the industry can grow from there.

Jordan Isenstadt: You both make great points. Banking is one of the biggest barriers to the industry's success, so banks investing will be huge. As for the Super Bowl, a couple companies have tried to get cannabis ads in and it hasn't happened yet, but this past Super Bowl there was a non-NFL-affiliated cannabis consumption event our client Dutchie was involved with. It's coming, baby steps — I think we're probably five to ten years away from some of that.

Bryan Fields: Sooner, I hope — I've been on record with predictions for years, and it's always 'five years.'

Kellan Finney: What would make it for Bryan is Aaron Rodgers and the New York Jets winning the Super Bowl with a cannabis ad airing during the game.

Bryan Fields: I'm going to try to speak that into existence right now.

Jordan Isenstadt: I don't know if you're a Jets fan — he's becoming a football fan, a transitioning football fan. I've told you my football story with my son — it's awesome as a parent to impart things on your kids, but in this case my son got into football and taught me football; I was never into it before. So my football allegiance is weird — he's a Packers fan, so I'm a Packers fan, which makes no sense given my Jets/Mets New York roots. And remember, Snoop Dogg smoked weed on camera at the Super Bowl a couple years ago during the big hip-hop halftime showcase, so people don't expect as big a shock from someone like him.

Bryan Fields: Jordan, if our listeners want to get in touch, want to learn more, and need help with PR, where can they find you?

Jordan Isenstadt: You can find us at Marino's website, the email is cannabis@marino.com, and you can find me on LinkedIn — Mr. Isenstadt. That's the social channel I use most, and a lot of what I post there showcases our latest and greatest hits and accomplishments for our clients.

Bryan Fields: Awesome, we'll link it in the show notes. Thanks for taking the time, this was a lot of fun.

Jordan Isenstadt: Thanks, Bryan.
summary: In this episode of The Dime, hosts Bryan Fields and Kellan Finney sit down with Jordan Isenstadt, Senior VP at PR and marketing agency Marino, to trace how he built one of the cannabis industry's leading PR practices from a chance connection with Curaleaf's predecessor, PalliaTech, and to unpack the real differences between earned, owned, and paid media in a heavily stigmatized, federally illegal industry. The conversation shifts into a candid, personal discussion about cannabis and parenting — how Jordan's own upbringing with cannabis-tolerant parents shapes how he talks to his 12- and 8-year-olds, whether gummies are a risky formulation around kids, and whether proactive, honest conversations (rather than DARE-style scare tactics) are the better path forward. The episode closes with rapid-fire predictions on federal legalization, banking, and a hypothetical Super Bowl cannabis ad as true markers of destigmatization.
takeaways: Jordan Isenstadt built Marino's cannabis PR practice starting in 2017 after noticing New York's nascent medical program lacked professional PR support, growing it through a serendipitous early client relationship with PalliaTech, which later became Curaleaf.

PR's core specialty is 'earned media' (per the PESO model: paid, earned, shared/social, owned) — unpaid third-party coverage that builds credibility and validation, distinct from paid ads or owned content like websites and social media.

Because of federal prohibition and inconsistent state-by-state advertising regulations, earned media and storytelling are disproportionately important marketing tools for cannabis brands compared to other industries.

New York's social equity licensing structure means many new dispensary owners come from the legacy market and are unaccustomed to speaking publicly about their business, requiring extensive media training and trust-building from PR teams.

Jordan's personal experience trying cannabis at 15 with eventual parental involvement shapes his belief that proactive, honest, non-scare-tactic conversations with kids (ideally around middle school) are more effective than programs like D.A.R.E.
Both hosts and the guest raise concerns that cannabis gummies may be too kid-friendly as a formulation, given documented incidents of children accidentally consuming edibles.

Predictions for when cannabis stigma will truly end vary: federal legalization and safe banking (Jordan), major banks like Wells Fargo or Bank of America investing capital (Kellan), and a cannabis commercial airing during the Super Bowl (Bryan).

faq.question: What is the difference between earned, owned, and paid media in PR?
faq.answer: Earned media is unpaid third-party coverage (podcasts, print, broadcast) that builds credibility; paid media is advertising you pay an outlet for; owned media is content you control directly, like your website, blog, or social media. Most brands need a healthy mix of all three, but in cannabis, earned media is especially valuable because federal prohibition limits traditional paid advertising options.

faq.question: Why is PR especially important for cannabis brands compared to other industries?
faq.answer: Because cannabis remains federally illegal, traditional advertising and paid marketing channels (like many ad platforms and publishers) are restricted or inconsistent from state to state, making earned media and authentic storytelling one of the most viable ways for cannabis brands to build visibility and trust.

faq.question: How did Jordan Isenstadt get Marino into the cannabis PR business?
faq.answer: In 2017, while personally getting a medical cannabis card in New York, Jordan recognized the industry needed PR support. He pitched Marino's leadership with research on New York's medical operators, and the practice took off after a chance connection with Ed Conklin, who had moved from McDonald's to PalliaTech (which became Curaleaf), leading to a long corporate PR relationship as the company expanded from 5 to 19 states.

faq.question: Why do many New York dispensary owners struggle with public-facing PR and media training?
faq.answer: New York structured its adult-use licensing to prioritize justice-involved and social equity applicants, many of whom came from the legacy cannabis market and are used to operating discreetly rather than speaking publicly about their business, tech, leases, or teams, so they often need more extensive media training than corporate cannabis executives.

faq.question: What approach does Jordan Isenstadt recommend for talking to kids about cannabis?
faq.answer: He favors proactive, honest conversations — ideally around middle school when peers and phones introduce the topic — focused on responsible use rather than scare tactics, similar to how parents might discuss alcohol responsibility, since scare-tactic programs like D.A.R.E. historically backfired.

faq.question: Are cannabis gummies a risky product formulation around children?
faq.answer: The episode raises concern that gummies, while commercially popular, closely resemble candy and may be too kid-friendly, given real incidents of children accidentally consuming a parent's edible stash; alternative formulations like pills are suggested as potentially safer around kids.

faq.question: What milestones would signal that cannabis stigma has truly ended?
faq.answer: Guest and hosts point to federal legalization and safe banking access, major banks like Wells Fargo or Bank of America investing significant capital into cannabis companies, and a cannabis brand airing a commercial during the Super Bowl as key cultural and financial turning points.

faq.question: What is the PESO model referenced in the episode?
faq.answer: PESO stands for Paid, Earned, Shared (social), and Owned media — a framework PR professionals use to categorize the different channels through which a brand's message reaches its audience.
